# Exercises

Each exercise is a small program. Try it before reading the solution under it. The solutions are complete `fn main` programs in edition 2024.

## Chapter 1 — How Iterators Work

Build an iterator that yields `0, 1, 4, 9, ...` and take the first five squares. Confirm that a `map` which increments a counter does not run before `collect`.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    struct Squares {
        n: i32,
    }
    impl Iterator for Squares {
        type Item = i32;
        fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
            let out = self.n * self.n;
            self.n += 1;
            Some(out)
        }
    }

    let first: Vec<_> = Squares { n: 0 }.take(5).collect();
    assert_eq!(first, [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]);

    let calls = Cell::new(0);
    let lazy = [1, 2, 3].into_iter().map(|n| {
        calls.set(calls.get() + 1);
        n
    });
    assert_eq!(calls.get(), 0);
    let _owned: Vec<_> = lazy.collect();
    assert_eq!(calls.get(), 3);
}
```

## Chapter 2 — Choosing the Right Iterator

Uppercase a `Vec<String>` without moving the vector, then append `!` in place.

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut names = vec![String::from("ada"), String::from("linus")];
    let labels: Vec<String> = names.iter().map(|name| name.to_uppercase()).collect();
    for name in &mut names {
        name.push('!');
    }
    assert_eq!(labels, ["ADA", "LINUS"]);
    assert_eq!(names, ["ada!", "linus!"]);
}
```

## Chapter 3 — Lazy Evaluation

From `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`, keep numbers greater than `3`, and take two of them. Count how many predicate calls run. It should be less than six if `take` stops the pull. Work out the count before you run it: `filter` must see `1, 2, 3, 4, 5` to produce two hits, and `6` is never pulled.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::cell::Cell;

    let checks = Cell::new(0);
    let kept: Vec<_> = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
        .into_iter()
        .filter(|n| {
            checks.set(checks.get() + 1);
            *n > 3
        })
        .take(2)
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(kept, [4, 5]);
    assert_eq!(checks.get(), 5);
}
```

## Chapter 4 — Transforming Data

Split `"a,b;c"` on `;`, then on `,`, and collect the three letters. Zip them with `1..` and stop at the shorter side. There is no fourth number.

```rust
fn main() {
    let text = "a,b;c";
    let letters: Vec<&str> = text.split(';').flat_map(|part| part.split(',')).collect();
    let pairs: Vec<_> = letters.iter().copied().zip(1..).collect();
    assert_eq!(letters, ["a", "b", "c"]);
    assert_eq!(pairs, [("a", 1), ("b", 2), ("c", 3)]);
}
```

## Chapter 5 — Filtering and Selecting

Parse `["3", "x", "5", "8", "1"]`, drop failures, skip the first success, and then take while the number is greater than `4`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let raw = ["3", "x", "5", "8", "1"];
    let kept: Vec<i32> = raw
        .iter()
        .filter_map(|text| text.parse().ok())
        .skip(1)
        .take_while(|n| *n > 4)
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(kept, [5, 8]);
}
```

The successes are `3, 5, 8, 1`. `skip(1)` drops `3`. `take_while` keeps `5` and `8`, then stops at `1` without including it.

## Chapter 6 — Aggregating and Consuming

Sum the even readings with `filter` and `sum`. Separately, `fold` the same slice into the maximum, with a start of `i32::MIN`.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [3, 8, 1, 8, 4];
    let even_sum: i32 = readings.iter().copied().filter(|n| n % 2 == 0).sum();
    assert_eq!(even_sum, 20);

    let max = readings.iter().copied().fold(i32::MIN, i32::max);
    assert_eq!(max, 8);
}
```

## Chapter 7 — Composing Pipelines

Normalize `[" Bob ", "ada", "bob"]` to lowercase trimmed strings, keep first-seen order, and count how many were dropped as duplicates.

```rust
fn main() {
    use std::collections::HashSet;

    let raw = [" Bob ", "ada", "bob"];
    let mut seen = HashSet::new();
    let mut dropped = 0;
    let names: Vec<String> = raw
        .iter()
        .map(|text| text.trim().to_lowercase())
        .filter(|name| {
            if seen.insert(name.clone()) {
                true
            } else {
                dropped += 1;
                false
            }
        })
        .collect();
    assert_eq!(names, ["bob", "ada"]);
    assert_eq!(dropped, 1);
}
```

## Chapter 8 — Implementing Iterator

Write an iterator over the even indices of a borrowed slice: index `0`, then `2`, then `4`.

```rust
struct Evens<'a, T> {
    slice: &'a [T],
    index: usize,
}

impl<'a, T> Iterator for Evens<'a, T> {
    type Item = &'a T;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        let item = self.slice.get(self.index)?;
        self.index += 2;
        Some(item)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let readings = [10, 11, 12, 13, 14];
    let even: Vec<i32> = Evens { slice: &readings, index: 0 }.copied().collect();
    assert_eq!(even, [10, 12, 14]);
}
```

## Chapter 9 — Custom Adaptors

Write an adaptor that yields items until it has seen `limit` items that pass a predicate, and also yields the ones that fail, but stops entirely once the passing count is reached. The item that hits the limit is included.

A simpler brief that still practices state: yield items, but stop after the running sum reaches `10`, including the item that crossed it.

```rust
struct UntilSum<I> {
    inner: I,
    sum: i32,
    limit: i32,
    done: bool,
}

impl<I> Iterator for UntilSum<I>
where
    I: Iterator<Item = i32>,
{
    type Item = i32;

    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item> {
        if self.done {
            return None;
        }
        let n = self.inner.next()?;
        self.sum += n;
        if self.sum >= self.limit {
            self.done = true;
        }
        Some(n)
    }
}

fn main() {
    let kept: Vec<_> = UntilSum {
        inner: [3, 4, 5, 100].into_iter(),
        sum: 0,
        limit: 10,
        done: false,
    }
    .collect();
    assert_eq!(kept, [3, 4, 5]);
}
```

`3 + 4 + 5` is `12`, which crosses `10`, so `5` is included. The next call sees `done` and returns `None` without pulling `100`.

## Chapter 14 — Error Handling in Pipelines

Parse integers and return the first error as `String`. A second function should skip errors.

```rust
fn fail_fast(fields: &[&str]) -> Result<Vec<i32>, String> {
    fields
        .iter()
        .map(|text| text.parse::<i32>().map_err(|err| format!("{text}: {err}")))
        .collect()
}

fn skip_bad(fields: &[&str]) -> Vec<i32> {
    fields.iter().filter_map(|text| text.parse().ok()).collect()
}

fn main() {
    assert!(fail_fast(&["1", "x", "3"]).is_err());
    assert_eq!(fail_fast(&["1", "3"]).unwrap(), [1, 3]);
    assert_eq!(skip_bad(&["1", "x", "3"]), [1, 3]);
}
```

## Chapter 11 — Performance

Rewrite a sum so it does not allocate a `Vec` of doubled values. Keep the result.

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
    let total: i32 = readings.iter().map(|n| n * 2).sum();
    assert_eq!(total, 30);
}
```

That is the whole exercise. If a profile shows `alloc`, look for a `collect` that exists only to call `sum` or `any` on the result.
